To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the number of times a person looks at a light that never changes in a situation where a change in the light indicates a need of a friend is significantly greater than the number of looks when a stranger is in the same situation, and the number of looks is significantly greater when a stranger is involved than when a friend is involved in a situation where the change in the light means the other person has made a substantial contribution.
people keep better track of the needs and inputs of friends than of strangers and keep better track of strangers' inputs than friends' inputs.
people keep track of others' needs and inputs, and that the amount of keeping track depends on the relationship between the two people.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of attention in the development and maintenance of social relationships.
the effects of the social situation on the information processing of the individual.
how the nature of the social relationship between individuals affects their perception and behavior toward one another.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
subjects keep track of the inputs and needs of friends and strangers differently.
keeping track of another's needs is greater when the other is a friend, while keeping track of another' inputs is greater when the relationship is with a stranger.
keeping track of needs and inputs is a function of the nature of the relationship between the individuals involved and the nature of the task in question.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the distinction between communal (friend) and exchange (stranger) relationships is important in understanding how we keep track of other people.
we have shown that the distinction between communal versus exchange relationships is useful in understanding the social cognition and behavior of people.
we found support for a distinction between communal and market relationships and that we have identified a number of ways that people keep track of their relationships.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the eye-tracking technology to understand the social dynamics between people.
we need to keep track of the needs and inputs of others in our social world, but that this tracking depends on the relationship we have with them.

people do not keep track of the inputs they make to a task in the same way that they keep track of the needs and inputs of others, and that this is true even when the inputs they have made are substantial and salient.
